transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, I'm here because... it's about the datasets. I’m pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions. They're deliberately planting errors in the data to make it look like I can’t lead the work anymore. Which is ridiculous, because modeling is just... well, it's all about isolating variables. 

Like when we were doing that groundwater study a few years back. The rain that spring was incredible. Actually, the rain last week was pretty bad too, it completely flooded out my tomato plants in the backyard. I tried building a raised bed for them this year, using this nice cedar wood I found on sale at the hardware store, but the soil drainage just wasn't right. You really have to get the drainage right or the roots just rot out completely, and then you've wasted the whole season. I told my wife we should have just planted peppers instead, they're a lot more forgiving... 

But anyway, she and the junior analysts at work keep telling me it’s just version-control mistakes with the files. The errors, I mean. But I know what I'm looking at. They're planting them.
Have you been feeling unusually energized or unusually irritable lately?

Energized? No, I don't think so. I haven't been running marathons or anything. And irritable... well, I don't think I'm any more irritable than usual. I mean, sure, I get annoyed when things don't work right. Like the toaster we have in the kitchen. It's one of those four-slice ones, but the left side just burns everything on the edges while the middle stays completely soft. It's a thermal distribution issue, obviously. The heating elements are spaced too far apart. 

I took it apart last weekend to see if I could recalibrate the thermostat switch, but they use these proprietary security screws now. Star-shaped with a little pin in the middle. You have to buy a special bit set just to fix your own appliances, which is a complete scam if you ask me. I ended up having to drive all the way to the auto parts store to find the right bit, and the traffic on the interstate was backed up for three miles because of some fender bender near the overpass. I used to take the back roads to avoid all that, but they put in those new traffic calming speed bumps, and it just ruins your suspension over time... 

But anyway, no, I wouldn't say I'm unusually energized or irritable. Just dealing with the usual things, you know?
Have you been seeing things that other people can’t see?

Seeing things? No, no, my vision is fine. I mean, I wear reading glasses now, the little half-moon ones, because the text on those contour maps they send over gets so small. It's like they're trying to cram too much topographical data onto one sheet. 

I was actually looking at a map of the old county reservoir the other day. They drained it back in '98, I think. Or maybe '99. We used to take the kids fishing there when they were little. You could catch these massive largemouth bass right off the eastern bank if you used the right spinnerbait. The trick was to cast right near the submerged tree stumps. My son caught one that must have been four pounds. We tried to mount it, but the taxidermist in town—old guy named Earl—he retired and moved down to Florida. Gulf Coast, I think. Sarasota maybe? The humidity down there is terrible for the joints, though. I have a buddy who moved to Tampa and he says his knees ache every time a storm rolls in off the water... 

But no, I don't see anything that isn't there. Just the regular stuff. The data. The errors they're leaving for me.
Do you ever feel like other people can hear your thoughts?

Hear my thoughts? No, I don't think so. That's... that's not how the brain works, scientifically speaking. It's all electrical impulses and synapses, contained in the skull. 

Although, speaking of skulls, I was reading this fascinating article the other day about phrenology. You know, that old pseudoscience where they thought the bumps on your head told you about your personality? Completely debunked, obviously. But the history of it is wild. They used to have these special calipers to measure the skull. I actually saw a pair of antique calipers at a flea market last month. I almost bought them, but the guy wanted fifty dollars, and the brass was completely tarnished. I know a trick for polishing brass using ketchup and a little bit of salt—the acidity in the tomatoes really eats through the oxidation. My grandmother taught me that. She used to have this huge collection of brass candlesticks that she kept lined up on the mantle above the fireplace. The fireplace was brick, real solid masonry, not like the fake veneer stuff they put on houses nowadays. You can always tell the fake stuff because the mortar lines are too perfect, you know? 

But anyway, no. Nobody can hear what I'm thinking. That's just... that's not possible. They just track the revisions.
Have you had any recent head injury, seizure, or other neurological illness?

Head injury? No, no seizures or anything like that. My head is perfectly fine. I haven't hit it on anything, anyway. I'm actually very careful about that sort of thing, especially when I'm doing work around the house. 

A lot of guys my age get hurt falling off ladders when they're cleaning out their gutters. It's a simple physics problem, really—the center of gravity shifts too far past the base of support, the angle of the ladder slips, and down you go. I actually bought one of those telescoping aluminum wands for the garden hose so I can flush the gutters right from the ground. It uses a specialized nozzle to increase the velocity of the water. The pressure in our neighborhood is usually around 60 PSI, which is decent, but you really notice a drop around six in the evening when everybody's sprinkler systems kick on. 

The city water authority just installed these new smart meters last fall to track all that peak usage. They transmit the data using a low-frequency radio signal, which is pretty efficient. I was looking at the technical specs for the frequency bands they use, and it's right on the edge of the old amateur radio bands. I used to mess around with HAM radio back in the eighties. I had this massive Yagi antenna up on the roof. I ended up having to take it down after a bad windstorm bent the main mast, though. Aluminum tubing just can't withstand sustained sheer force like that without proper guy wires. 

But, uh... yeah, no head injuries or neurological problems. I'm fine in that department.
How long have you been convinced that your coworkers are planting errors in the data?

How long? Well, I'd say... it's been about two months. I know for sure because the certainty that people on the project are tracking my revisions and planting those errors really started right around the time I had to requisition a new office chair. The hydraulic cylinder on my old one gave out, so it would just slowly sink toward the floor while I was running my statistical models. It's a simple pneumatic mechanism, really, just pressurized nitrogen gas, but once the rubber seal degrades, it's completely useless. 

I ended up having to order this new mesh-back chair, and the shipping took forever. You know, most of that commercial office furniture is manufactured overseas, and the logistics of maritime shipping are just fascinating. The container ships get backed up at the ports, and they just sit there idling. The scheduling algorithms they use to manage the cargo offloading are incredibly complex, relying on dynamic programming to optimize the crane movements. I actually tried to explain the math behind it to my neighbor, Gary, but he wasn't interested. Gary's more of a car guy. He's been restoring a '69 Chevelle in his garage for the better part of a decade. He finally got the engine block machined last week. It's a 396 cubic inch V8. Beautiful piece of engineering, though carbureted engines are terribly inefficient compared to modern electronic fuel injection. The fuel-to-air ratio is just never quite optimal, especially when the ambient temperature drops... 

But, uh, yes. Two months. That's how long they've been doing it.
Have you had this belief that your coworkers are planting errors for more than one month?

Well, yes, like I just said, it's definitely been more than a month. The certainty that people on the project are tracking my revisions and planting those errors has been there for about the last two months. 

I know because I mark everything down on my desk calendar. It's one of those big paper blotter calendars with the faux-leather corners. You don't see those much anymore, really, because everyone relies on digital calendars now. But the problem with digital calendars is the server synchronization. If there's a latency issue between the local client and the exchange server, you can get conflicting data. The timestamp protocols—like NTP, Network Time Protocol—are supposed to prevent that by keeping all the system clocks synced to within milliseconds of Coordinated Universal Time. They use these atomic clocks, usually cesium or rubidium, which measure the exact electromagnetic radiation of electron transitions. It's incredibly precise. I read a paper recently explaining that the primary atomic clock in Colorado is so accurate it won't lose a single second in a hundred million years. 

A hundred million years... it really makes you wonder what the earth's topography will even look like then. Because tectonic plate drift averages about one and a half centimeters a year, depending on the fault line, so over a hundred million years, the continents will be completely unrecognizable. The Pacific Ocean might just close up entirely, pushing California right up against Japan. The subduction zones would create massive volcanic activity... 

But, uh, yes. More than a month. Two months.
Have you ever had a period when you needed much less sleep than usual and still felt full of energy?

Less sleep? No, no, I don't think so. I usually get my seven or eight hours. I've never really had a time where I didn't need to sleep and still felt energized. Sleep is actually a fascinating biological imperative. The circadian rhythm is governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the hypothalamus, which responds to light cues. It regulates the secretion of melatonin from the pineal gland. 

I actually bought these blackout curtains for my bedroom a few years ago to optimize my sleep architecture. The fabric has this specialized thermal backing woven into it. It's supposedly a patented polymer blend designed to block 99% of UV light and insulate against heat transfer. Thermal dynamics in residential architecture is a really overlooked field. Most heat loss in a standard single-family home occurs through poorly sealed fenestrations. You can actually calculate the R-value of a window by measuring the thermal resistance of the glazing assembly. I borrowed an infrared thermal imaging camera from the university physics department once just to map the heat signature of my house in the middle of winter. The color gradients on those thermograms are really quite striking, especially when you see the bright red heat blooms escaping right through the aluminum window frames. Aluminum is a terrible insulator, obviously, because of its high thermal conductivity. It's great for heat sinks in computer processors, though. 

But, uh, no. I haven't had any periods where I needed less sleep.
Aside from this issue with the data, have you been having trouble functioning at work?

Well, yes, actually. I've fallen pretty far behind on my modeling deliverables. It's gotten to the point where the firm had to reassign pieces of my contract to other people. And I'm supposed to be supervising these junior analysts, but I've basically stopped being useful to them. It's just hard to focus when... well, and at home, I mostly keep to myself. My wife has really had to push me just to keep basic routines going, like eating and showering. 

Speaking of showering, the municipal water pressure in our neighborhood has been fluctuating wildly lately. It's a real problem with aging infrastructure. Most of the subterranean water mains in this city were laid down in the 1950s using cast iron pipes, which are highly susceptible to internal corrosion and tuberculation. That's when these little mineral deposits build up inside the pipe and restrict the flow rate. The fluid dynamics of it are fascinating, really. According to Bernoulli's principle, as the diameter of the pipe decreases due to the buildup, the velocity of the water increases, but the pressure actually drops. 

The city is supposed to be replacing them with high-density polyethylene, HDPE, which is much more resilient. It's a thermoplastic polymer made from petroleum, and the molecular structure makes it incredibly resistant to impact and chemicals. They use a process called horizontal directional drilling to install it, which is so much more efficient than the old open-cut trenching methods. They just bore a subterranean tunnel and pull the continuous pipe right through. I was watching a crew do it down the street last month. The drill operator has this specialized tracking device to monitor the pitch and roll of the drill head underground. It uses electromagnetic sondes... 

But, uh, yes. I have been having trouble functioning. At work and at home.
Have you been feeling depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed? No, I don't think so. I wouldn't say I feel sad or down most of the day. I'm mostly just preoccupied with the data inconsistencies at work. My mood itself is actually fairly stable. 

Not like the barometric pressure this week, which has been all over the place. It's fascinating how atmospheric pressure systems operate, really. The pressure differentials are entirely governed by the Navier-Stokes equations, which are just foundational to fluid dynamics. They describe the motion of viscous fluid substances. It's actually one of the Millennium Prize Problems, you know. The Clay Mathematics Institute offered a million dollars to anyone who can mathematically prove the existence and smoothness of solutions in three dimensions. The difficulty lies entirely in the non-linear turbulence. Turbulence is just chaotic changes in pressure and flow velocity. You see it everywhere, from global weather patterns to the aerodynamic wake of a commercial airliner. 

A Boeing 777, for instance, creates massive wingtip vortices. It's a byproduct of lift, where the high-pressure air beneath the wing seeks the low-pressure area above it, creating these violent horizontal tornadoes that can linger in the air for miles. That's exactly why air traffic controllers have to enforce strict wake turbulence separation minima between heavy aircraft and smaller planes. If a little Cessna flies into a 777's wake, the induced roll can completely overwhelm the aircraft's control authority. The physics of it are just unforgiving...

But, uh, no. I haven't been feeling depressed.
Have you been hearing voices when no one else is around?

Voices? No, no, I haven't heard any voices. The house is usually quite silent when I'm alone. Well, except for the ambient noise, of course. True silence is actually quite rare. The threshold of human hearing is generally considered to be zero decibels, but that's just a reference point for a sound wave with a pressure of 20 micropascals. 

I was reading about anechoic chambers recently. They're these highly specialized rooms designed to completely absorb reflections of either sound or electromagnetic waves. They line the walls, floor, and ceiling with these deep, wedge-shaped fiberglass acoustic absorbers. The geometry of the wedges is critical because it forces the sound waves to bounce back and forth deep within the structure of the foam, dissipating the acoustic energy as trace amounts of heat. Microsoft actually built the quietest place on Earth at their headquarters in Washington. The background noise level there is negative 20.6 decibels. It's so quiet that you can hear your own heartbeat, the blood rushing through your veins, and even the grinding of your bones when you move. It's fascinating, but people who go in there often start experiencing sensory deprivation hallucinations within just a few minutes. The brain is essentially a pattern-recognition engine, and when you deprive it of external stimuli, it just starts generating its own internal signals to compensate. It's the same mechanism behind phantom limb pain in amputees. The somatosensory cortex is still looking for input from the missing limb, and when it doesn't get any, it creates the sensation of pain...

But, um, no. To answer your question, I haven't been hearing any voices.
Have you started using any new drugs or medications in the past few months?

New drugs? No, no new medications or anything like that. I just take my regular blood pressure pill, the same one I've been on for years. 

Speaking of pharmaceuticals, the pharmacokinetic modeling involved in drug development is just astounding these days. They use these massive compartmental models to simulate how a compound distributes through the body's tissues over time. The rate of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion—the ADME profile—is all governed by differential equations. It's really just a specialized application of mass transfer kinetics. The liver, for instance, acts as this incredible biochemical reactor. The cytochrome P450 enzymes in the hepatic cells are responsible for metabolizing the vast majority of xenobiotics. They catalyze the oxidation of organic substances. The molecular docking simulations they run now to predict how a new drug molecule will bind to those enzyme active sites require immense computational power. They use Monte Carlo algorithms to sample all the possible conformational states of the protein-ligand complex. It's basically a highly sophisticated optimization problem, trying to find the lowest free energy state of the system. 

It reminds me of the protein folding problem, actually. For decades, it was considered computationally intractable to predict a protein's three-dimensional structure just from its amino acid sequence. The number of possible conformations is astronomically large—Levinthal's paradox, they call it. If a protein tried every possible fold sequentially, it would take longer than the age of the universe to find the right one. But in reality, they fold in milliseconds. Now, with deep learning models like AlphaFold, they've practically solved it using attention-based neural networks...

But, uh, no. I haven't started any new medications. Just the usual ones.
Have you found yourself feeling much less motivated than usual to do things?

Motivated? Well, I suppose I have been. These days I can just sit for hours at my desk, or out in the garage with the telescope still covered. I know I used to enjoy things, you know, hiking, mentoring the younger analysts at the office, going to the local astronomy nights... but lately I just don’t feel much pull to start anything or talk to anyone. 

The telescope just sits there under its tarp. It's a Schmidt-Cassegrain design. Beautiful piece of engineering, really. It uses a catadioptric optical system, which combines a primary spherical mirror with a secondary convex mirror and a refractive corrector plate to eliminate spherical aberration. Spherical aberration is a fascinating optical flaw. It happens when incoming parallel light rays striking the outer edges of a spherical mirror focus at a slightly different point along the optical axis than the rays striking the center. It completely ruins the image resolution, creating this soft, blurred halo effect. 

That's exactly what happened with the Hubble Space Telescope when it was first deployed in 1990. The primary mirror was ground incorrectly by just 2.2 micrometers—literally a fraction of a wavelength of red light. Perkin-Elmer, the contractor, had a flawed null corrector device during the manufacturing process. They had to send up a space shuttle mission to install corrective optics, the COSTAR system, which essentially acted like a highly complex pair of glasses for the telescope. The precision required for the orbital rendezvous maneuvers on that servicing mission is just staggering. You have to calculate the Hohmann transfer orbits using Kepler's laws of planetary motion, and the delta-v requirements have to be perfectly optimized to conserve propellant. The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation dictates the exact mass ratio needed, which is an exponential function of the required velocity change divided by the exhaust velocity... 

But, um... anyway. Yeah. I just don't feel the pull to take the cover off it anymore. Or do much of anything else, really.
Do you feel emotionally flat or unable to experience much pleasure lately?

Emotionally flat? I guess... I guess you could say that. It's like I was just saying about the telescope and the hiking and the astronomy nights. I used to really get a kick out of those things, especially mentoring the younger analysts at the office. Seeing them grasp a complex concept for the first time... it used to feel good. Now I just don't feel much pull to start anything or talk to anyone. I can just sit for hours at my desk or out in the garage, and I don't really feel... anything about it.

It's curious, really, the concept of feeling "flat." In mathematics, a flat surface—a Euclidean plane—has zero Gaussian curvature. It's the simplest two-dimensional manifold. The intrinsic geometry of a flat space means that the sum of the angles in any triangle will always be exactly 180 degrees, and parallel lines will never intersect. But when you move into non-Euclidean geometries, everything changes. On a sphere, which has positive curvature, the angles of a triangle add up to more than 180 degrees. And on a hyperbolic paraboloid—a saddle shape with negative curvature—they add up to less. 

The topology of the universe itself is still a matter of debate among cosmologists. Is it flat, open, or closed? The cosmic microwave background radiation data from the Planck satellite suggests that the observable universe is incredibly close to being spatially flat, with a margin of error of just about 0.4 percent. This flatness problem was actually one of the main catalysts for the theory of cosmic inflation. If the early universe underwent an exponential expansion in a fraction of a second, it would have stretched out any initial curvature, making the universe appear flat to us today, much like how the Earth appears flat from our localized perspective on the surface. The scalar field driving that inflation, the inflaton field, would have to have very specific potential energy properties to roll down the energy curve at just the right rate...

But, uh, yes. Emotionally, I suppose I do feel quite flat. I just don't experience that pleasure anymore.
For at least six months, have you been having ongoing problems like this — with the belief about your coworkers or with becoming withdrawn and emotionally flat?

Well, let's see... six months? No, it's been quite a bit longer than that. This whole... decline, I suppose you could call it, really started after I was put in charge of the larger environmental modeling contract. That was about two years and two months ago. 

Environmental modeling is such a complex undertaking. You're dealing with coupled non-linear partial differential equations to simulate fluid dynamics in the atmosphere and oceans. The Navier-Stokes equations, for instance, are notoriously difficult to solve. They describe the motion of viscous fluid substances, and the existence and smoothness of solutions to these equations in three dimensions is actually one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems in mathematics. If you can prove it, the Clay Mathematics Institute will give you a million dollars. 

The turbulence modeling is the real bottleneck. We use Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations, but you have to introduce turbulence models like the k-epsilon model to close the equations. It's essentially trying to predict the unpredictable. The chaotic nature of the system means that even minuscule changes in the initial conditions—like the famous butterfly effect coined by Edward Lorenz—can lead to vastly different outcomes over time. Lorenz was a meteorologist, you know, and he discovered strange attractors while running weather simulations on a Royal McBee LGP-30 computer in the 1960s. The Lorenz attractor looks like a butterfly, ironically enough. It's a fractal structure, meaning it has a non-integer dimension. Fractals are everywhere in nature—coastlines, snowflakes, the branching of blood vessels... 

But, um, yes. The contract. That was about two years and two months ago, and that's when this all started.
Have you ever heard a voice speaking to you when no one was there?

Voices? No... no, I haven't experienced anything like that. Just the normal ambient sounds, you know. 

Sound is an interesting phenomenon, though, when you really break it down. It's purely mechanical—longitudinal waves of pressure propagating through a medium like air or water. Unlike electromagnetic radiation, which can travel through the vacuum of space, sound absolutely requires matter to vibrate. The speed of sound in dry air at standard atmospheric pressure is roughly 343 meters per second, but that changes depending on the temperature and the density of the medium. In water, it's over four times faster. 

That's the fundamental principle behind sonar, actually—Sound Navigation and Ranging. Submarines use it to navigate and detect targets in the deep ocean. They send out an acoustic pulse, a 'ping', and measure the time it takes for the echo to return. If the target is moving, the frequency of the return echo will be altered due to the Doppler effect. Christian Doppler described that mathematically in 1842. It's the same reason an ambulance siren noticeably drops in pitch as it drives past you on the street. The sound waves get compressed as the vehicle approaches and stretched out as it recedes. We actually use the exact same principle in astrophysics, but with light waves instead of sound, to measure the redshift of distant galaxies. Edwin Hubble used the relativistic Doppler effect to prove the universe is expanding, which completely upended Einstein's cosmological constant... 

But, ah, to answer your question, no. I don't hear anyone speaking when there's nobody around. Just my own thoughts.
Before you became convinced your coworkers were planting errors, had you already been feeling withdrawn and emotionally flat?

Well, let me think about the timeline there. The certainty that people on the project are tracking my revisions and planting errors... that specific realization has been there for about the last two months. But before that? Yes, the withdrawal and the... the flatness, that was already happening. 

It's fascinating how timelines intersect, isn't it? Like the intersection of two non-parallel lines in a Euclidean plane. They have exactly one point in common. But if you consider lines in three-dimensional space, they can be skew lines—lines that are neither parallel nor intersecting. They exist in different planes entirely. The shortest distance between two skew lines can be calculated using the cross product of their directional vectors. 

Vectors are incredibly useful in physics. A vector has both magnitude and direction, unlike a scalar, which only has magnitude. Temperature is a scalar, but velocity is a vector. If you want to calculate the work done by a force, you take the dot product of the force vector and the displacement vector. The dot product yields a scalar, which is why work is measured in Joules, a scalar quantity. James Prescott Joule, the English brewer and physicist, established the mechanical equivalent of heat in the 1840s. He used a falling weight to spin a paddle wheel in an insulated barrel of water, proving that mechanical work could be converted directly into thermal energy. It was a crucial step in formulating the First Law of Thermodynamics, the conservation of energy...

But, yes. The flatness was definitely there before I realized what they were doing with the errors. The errors started about two months ago.
Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually euphoric or overly confident?

Euphoric? No, I wouldn't say that. I've never really been the overly confident type, either. I just try to stick to the data, you know? 

Data is the foundation of everything we do. Without empirical evidence, we're just guessing. Sir Francis Bacon really championed the scientific method in the late 16th century—inductive reasoning, observing nature to formulate general principles. Before that, it was mostly Aristotelian deduction, starting from a premise and working down, which can be incredibly flawed if your initial premise is wrong. Aristotle thought heavier objects fell faster than lighter ones, which was accepted as fact for almost two thousand years until Galileo supposedly dropped the spheres from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Whether he actually did that or if it's just a thought experiment is still debated by historians, but the principle holds. Acceleration due to gravity is independent of mass in a vacuum. It's roughly 9.8 meters per second squared on Earth. 

Of course, if you go to the moon, it's only about one-sixth of that. The Apollo astronauts had to learn how to walk all over again in that low-gravity environment. The Apollo guidance computer was an absolute marvel of engineering, by the way. It used core rope memory, woven by hand by women in textile factories. They called it "LOL memory"—Little Old Lady memory. It was incredibly robust, completely immune to radiation, which is critical when you're passing through the Van Allen radiation belts... 

But, um, no. I've never had a period of euphoria or anything like that. Just steady work.
At any time since these problems began, have you had a period when you felt unusually energized?

Energized? No... no, I wouldn't say that. My energy levels are pretty consistent, really. Just the usual amount required to get through the day, you know? 

Energy is a fascinating concept, though, when you move away from the biological and look at the physical. In mechanics, energy is simply defined as the capacity to do work. You have potential energy—like a boulder sitting at the top of a hill—and kinetic energy, when that boulder is actually rolling down. The formula for kinetic energy is one-half mass times velocity squared. It’s very elegant in its simplicity. But then you get into electrical energy, which is what really runs our modern infrastructure. The whole War of the Currents in the late 1880s between Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla is a perfect example of... of commercial interests clashing with scientific optimization. Edison was pushing for direct current, DC, which is fine for short distances, but it suffers from severe voltage drop over long transmission lines. Tesla, who was backed by George Westinghouse, championed alternating current. With AC, you can use transformers to step up the voltage for long-distance transmission, which minimizes power loss, and then step it back down for safe residential use. The Chicago World's Fair in 1893 was completely illuminated by Westinghouse using Tesla's AC system, which pretty much proved its superiority once and for all. It completely changed the trajectory of human civilization... 

But, um... as for me, personally? No, no unusual energy. I just keep a steady pace.

doctor.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because I’m pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions and planting errors in the datasets to make it look like I can’t lead the work, even when my wife or the junior analysts tell me it’s just version-control mistakes.

The shortest distance between two skew lines can be calculated using the cross product of their directional vectors. 

Vectors are incredibly useful in physics. A vector has both magnitude and direction, unlike a scalar, which only has magnitude. Temperature is a scalar, but velocity is a vector. If you want to calculate the work done by a force, you take the dot product of the force vector and the displacement vector. The dot product yields a scalar, which is why work is measured in Joules, a scalar quantity. James Prescott Joule, the English brewer and physicist, established the mechanical equivalent of heat in the 1840s. He used a falling weight to spin a paddle wheel in an insulated barrel of water, proving that mechanical work could be converted directly into thermal energy. It was a crucial step in formulating the First Law of Thermodynamics, the conservation of energy...

But, yes. The flatness was definitely there before I realized what they were doing with the errors. The errors started about two months ago.

patient.answer:
Euphoric? No, I wouldn't say that. I've never really been the overly confident type, either. I just try to stick to the data, you know? 

Data is the foundation of everything we do. Without empirical evidence, we're just guessing. Sir Francis Bacon really championed the scientific method in the late 16th century—inductive reasoning, observing nature to formulate general principles. Before that, it was mostly Aristotelian deduction, starting from a premise and working down, which can be incredibly flawed if your initial premise is wrong. Aristotle thought heavier objects fell faster than lighter ones, which was accepted as fact for almost two thousand years until Galileo supposedly dropped the spheres from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Whether he actually did that or if it's just a thought experiment is still debated by historians, but the principle holds. Acceleration due to gravity is independent of mass in a vacuum. It's roughly 9.8 meters per second squared on Earth. 

Of course, if you go to the moon, it's only about one-sixth of that. The Apollo astronauts had to learn how to walk all over again in that low-gravity environment. The Apollo guidance computer was an absolute marvel of engineering, by the way. It used core rope memory, woven by hand by women in textile factories. They called it "LOL memory"—Little Old Lady memory. It was incredibly robust, completely immune to radiation, which is critical when you're passing through the Van Allen radiation belts... 

But, um, no. I've never had a period of euphoria or anything like that. Just steady work.

patient.answer:
Energized? No... no, I wouldn't say that. My energy levels are pretty consistent, really. Just the usual amount required to get through the day, you know? 

Energy is a fascinating concept, though, when you move away from the biological and look at the physical. In mechanics, energy is simply defined as the capacity to do work. You have potential energy—like a boulder sitting at the top of a hill—and kinetic energy, when that boulder is actually rolling down. The formula for kinetic energy is one-half mass times velocity squared. It’s very elegant in its simplicity. But then you get into electrical energy, which is what really runs our modern infrastructure. The whole War of the Currents in the late 1880s between Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla is a perfect example of... of commercial interests clashing with scientific optimization. Edison was pushing for direct current, DC, which is fine for short distances, but it suffers from severe voltage drop over long transmission lines. Tesla, who was backed by George Westinghouse, championed alternating current. With AC, you can use transformers to step up the voltage for long-distance transmission, which minimizes power loss, and then step it back down for safe residential use. The Chicago World's Fair in 1893 was completely illuminated by Westinghouse using Tesla's AC system, which pretty much proved its superiority once and for all. It completely changed the trajectory of human civilization... 

But, um... as for me, personally? No, no unusual energy. I just keep a steady pace.
